units.excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from powerful capabilities of foundation models.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is a set of protocols addressing severe risks from powerful foundation model capabilities.

units.excerpt: It is intended to complement Google’s existing suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enable AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
units.paraphrase: The Framework complements Google's existing AI safety practices and supports innovation consistent with its AI Principles.

units.excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.
units.paraphrase: The Framework draws on the wider discourse regarding Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.

units.excerpt: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
units.paraphrase: This introduces the list of core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.

units.context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Identify capability levels at which AI models without additional mitigations could pose severe risk
units.paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels at which unmitigated models could pose severe risk.

units.context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels
units.paraphrase: Another core component is implementing protocols to detect when such capability levels are reached.

units.context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Prepare and articulate mitigation plans in advance of when such capability levels are attained
units.paraphrase: Another core component is preparing mitigation plans before such capability levels are reached.

units.context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Where appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide our approach.
units.paraphrase: Another core component is involving external parties, where appropriate, to inform and guide the approach.

units.excerpt: In version 2.0 of the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which models may pose severe risks (which we call “Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)”), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
units.paraphrase: Version 2.0 specifies detection protocols for Critical Capability Levels and mitigation approaches for them.

units.excerpt: At present, the Framework primarily addresses misuse risk, but we also include an exploratory section addressing deceptive alignment risk, focusing on capability levels at which such risks may begin to arise.
units.paraphrase: The Framework mainly covers misuse risk but also has an exploratory section on deceptive alignment risk.

units.excerpt: For each type of risk, we define here a set of CCLs and a mitigation approach for them.
units.paraphrase: For each risk type, the document defines CCLs and a corresponding mitigation approach.

units.excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
units.paraphrase: Risk assessment must evaluate cross-cutting capabilities like agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

units.excerpt: The safety of frontier AI systems is a global public good.
units.paraphrase: Frontier AI safety is characterized as a global public good.

units.excerpt: The protocols here represent our current understanding and recommended approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
units.paraphrase: The protocols reflect the current understanding and recommended approach for anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

units.excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to AI systems reaching critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly applied across AI systems reaching critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: These mitigations should be understood as recommendations for the industry collectively: our adoption of them would only result in effective risk mitigation for society if all relevant organizations provide similar levels of protection, and our adoption of the protocols described in this Framework may depend on whether such organizations across the field adopt similar protocols.
units.paraphrase: The mitigations are framed as industry-wide recommendations, and Google's own adoption may depend on similar adoption by other organizations.

units.excerpt: The Framework is exploratory and based on early research.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is described as exploratory and grounded in early research.

units.excerpt: We may change our approach and recommendations over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
units.paraphrase: Google may revise its approach and recommendations as it gains more insight into future frontier model capabilities.

units.excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
units.paraphrase: Google commits to periodic review of the Framework and expects it to evolve substantially.

units.excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/blog/2023-09-26-rsp/, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy, https://openai.com/preparedness/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/updates/issue-brief-components-of-frontier-ai-safety-frameworks/,
units.paraphrase: A footnote listing external references on frontier AI safety practices.

units.excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
units.paraphrase: Misuse risk is defined as threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.

units.excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of highly autonomous systems purposefully undermining human control over AI systems.
units.paraphrase: Deceptive alignment risk is defined as highly autonomous systems purposefully undermining human control.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: delineating when such capability becomes present, and subsequently when the initial mitigation for this capability—automated monitoring—is no longer adequate.
units.paraphrase: This describes delineating when a capability arises and when automated monitoring, its initial mitigation, ceases to be adequate.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: We intend to evaluate our most powerful frontier models regularly to check whether their AI capabilities are approaching a CCL.
units.paraphrase: Google intends to regularly evaluate its most powerful frontier models to check proximity to a CCL.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: We also intend to evaluate any of these models that could indicate an exceptional increase in capabilities over previous models, and where appropriate, assess the likelihood of such capabilities and risks before and during training.
units.paraphrase: Google also intends to evaluate models showing exceptional capability increases and, where appropriate, assess risks before and during training.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: To do so, we will define a set of evaluations called “early warning evaluations,” with a specific “alert threshold” that flags when a CCL may be reached before the evaluations are run again.
units.paraphrase: Google will define early warning evaluations with alert thresholds flagging approaching CCLs before the next evaluation cycle.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to equip the model with appropriate scaffolding and other augmentations to make it more likely that we are also assessing the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations aim to equip models with scaffolding and augmentations so downstream system capabilities are also captured.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust the alert threshold of our evaluations if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
units.paraphrase: Google may increase evaluation frequency or adjust alert thresholds if progress suggests the safety buffer is insufficient.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: Where necessary, early warning evaluations may be supplemented by other evaluations to better understand model capabilities relative to our CCLs.
units.paraphrase: Additional evaluations may supplement early warning evaluations when needed to clarify capabilities relative to CCLs.

units.section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
units.excerpt: We may use additional external evaluators to test a model for relevant capabilities, if evaluators with relevant expertise are needed to provide an additional signal about a model’s proximity to CCLs.
units.paraphrase: External evaluators may be used to test models when specialized expertise is needed to gauge proximity to CCLs.

units.excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
units.paraphrase: Upon reaching an alert threshold, Google will assess proximity to the CCL and analyze risk, involving experts as needed.

units.excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.
units.paraphrase: The assessment informs the formulation and application of a response plan.

units.excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described later in this document.
units.paraphrase: Most response plans will center on applying the mitigations described later in the document.

units.excerpt: For misuse, we have two categories of mitigations: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and misuse filtering, detection, and response) intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in deployments.
units.paraphrase: Misuse mitigations fall into two categories: security mitigations preventing weight exfiltration, and deployment mitigations countering misuse in deployment.

units.excerpt: For deceptive alignment risk, automated monitoring may be applied to detect and respond to deceptive behavior for models that meet the first deceptive alignment CCL.
units.paraphrase: For deceptive alignment risk, automated monitoring may be used for models meeting the first deceptive alignment CCL.

units.excerpt: Note that these mitigations reflect considerations from the perspective of addressing severe risks from powerful capabilities alone; due to this focused scope, other risk management and security considerations may result in more stringent mitigations applied to a model than specified by the Framework.
units.paraphrase: The mitigations address only severe capability risks; other considerations may lead to stricter mitigations than the Framework specifies.

units.excerpt: A model flagged by an alert threshold may be assessed to pose risks for which readily available mitigations (including but not limited to those described below) may not be sufficient.
units.paraphrase: A flagged model may pose risks that available mitigations cannot sufficiently address.

units.excerpt: If this happens, the response plan may involve putting deployment or further development on hold until adequate mitigations can be applied.
units.paraphrase: In such cases, the response plan may pause deployment or development until adequate mitigations exist.

units.excerpt: Conversely, where model capabilities remain quite distant from a CCL, a response plan may involve the adoption of additional capability assessment processes to flag when heightened mitigations may be required.
units.paraphrase: If a model remains far from a CCL, the response plan may add capability assessment processes to flag when stronger mitigations are needed.

units.excerpt: The appropriateness and efficacy of applied mitigations should be reviewed periodically, drawing on information like related misuse or misuse attempt incidents; results from continued post-mitigation testing; statistics about our intelligence, monitoring and escalation processes; and updated threat modeling and risk landscape analysis.
units.paraphrase: Mitigation appropriateness and efficacy should be periodically reviewed using incident data, post-mitigation testing, monitoring statistics, and updated threat modeling.

units.excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse CCLs, as well as the mitigations that we provisionally assess as appropriate for them.
units.paraphrase: This introductory statement outlines that the Misuse section covers mitigation approach, misuse CCLs, and provisional appropriate mitigations.

units.excerpt: There are two categories of mitigations to address models with misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in deployments.
units.paraphrase: Misuse mitigations fall into security mitigations against exfiltration and deployment mitigations against misuse in deployment.

units.excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
units.paraphrase: Multiple levels of security mitigations allow calibrating robustness to the level of risk.

units.excerpt: For deployment mitigations, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
units.paraphrase: Deployment mitigations follow a standard process to apply, assess, and review measures calibrated to CCLs, reflecting their iterative nature.

units.excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration risk are important for models reaching CCLs.
units.paraphrase: Security mitigations against exfiltration are important for models that reach CCLs.

units.excerpt: This is because the release of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Weight release could allow removal of safeguards and give threat actors access to critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: Here, we rely on the RAND framework to articulate the level of security recommended for each CCL.
units.paraphrase: The RAND framework is used to articulate recommended security levels for each CCL.

units.excerpt: When we reference RAND security levels, we are referring to the security principles in their framework, rather than the benchmarks (i.e. concrete measures) also described in the RAND report.
units.paraphrase: References to RAND security levels denote the framework's security principles, not its concrete benchmark measures.

units.excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
units.paraphrase: As AI security is actively evolving research, the concrete measures for each security level are expected to change substantially.

units.excerpt: The following deployment mitigation process will be applied to models reaching a CCL, allowing for iterative and flexible tailoring of mitigations to each risk and use case.
units.paraphrase: A deployment mitigation process will be applied to models reaching a CCL, allowing flexible tailoring by risk and use case.

units.excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
units.paraphrase: Step one is developing and assessing mitigations, with safeguards and a safety case built through iteration.

units.context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
units.excerpt: Developing and improving a suite of safeguards targeting the capability. This includes, as appropriate, safety fine-tuning, misuse filtering and detection, and response protocols.
units.paraphrase: Sub-step: developing and improving safeguards targeting the capability, including fine-tuning, filtering, detection, and response protocols as appropriate.

units.context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
units.excerpt: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed through assurance evaluations and threat modeling research. The assessment takes the form of a safety case, taking into account factors such as the likelihood and consequences of misuse.
units.paraphrase: Sub-step: assessing mitigation robustness via assurance evaluations and threat modeling, producing a safety case considering likelihood and consequences of misuse.

units.excerpt: Pre-deployment review of safety case: general availability deployment of a model takes place only after the appropriate corporate governance body determines the safety case regarding each CCL the model has reached to be adequate.
units.paraphrase: Step two: general availability deployment occurs only after a corporate governance body deems the safety case for each reached CCL adequate.

units.excerpt: Post-deployment review of safety case: the safety case will be updated through red-teaming and revisions to our threat models.
units.paraphrase: Step three: the safety case is updated post-deployment via red-teaming and revised threat models.

units.excerpt: The safeguards for the model may be updated as well to ensure continued adequacy.
units.paraphrase: Model safeguards may also be updated to maintain continued adequacy.

units.excerpt: The table below details a set of CCLs we have identified through ongoing analysis of the CBRN, Cyber, and Machine Learning R&D risk domains.
units.paraphrase: The table describes CCLs identified from analysis of CBRN, Cyber, and Machine Learning R&D risk domains.

units.excerpt: We expect these to evolve over time.
units.paraphrase: The CCLs are expected to evolve over time.

units.excerpt: We recommend a security level to each of these CCLs, which reflect our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.
units.paraphrase: Each CCL is assigned a recommended security level reflecting the minimum appropriate security the frontier AI field should apply.

units.excerpt: In practice, our overall security posture may commonly exceed the baseline levels recommended here.
units.paraphrase: Actual security posture may often exceed the recommended baseline levels.

units.excerpt: These recommended security levels reflect our current thinking and may be adjusted if our empirical understanding of the risks changes.
units.paraphrase: Recommended security levels reflect current thinking and may be adjusted as empirical understanding evolves.

units.excerpt: This may occur if, for example, a model does not possess capabilities meaningfully different from other widely available models that have not demonstrably caused or contributed to severe risks, or if we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
units.paraphrase: Adjustment might occur if a model's capabilities aren't meaningfully different from other benign widely-available models, or if open release benefits are judged to outweigh risks.

units.excerpt: Relatedly, we believe these recommendations will only be effective if the entire frontier AI field applies them, and of limited social utility if not.
units.paraphrase: The recommendations are believed effective only if adopted across the entire frontier AI field.

units.excerpt: By "deceptive alignment," we mean the risk that AI systems purposefully undermine human control over AI systems.
units.paraphrase: Deceptive alignment is defined as AI systems purposefully undermining human control.

units.excerpt: While we do not express any opinion here about how likely it is for deceptive alignment to arise, this section’s provisions aim to prepare for this possibility.
units.paraphrase: No view is expressed on the likelihood of deceptive alignment, but the section aims to prepare for the possibility.

units.excerpt: Note that the effective mitigation of deceptive alignment risk requires the application of safeguards to all AI systems reaching critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Effective mitigation of deceptive alignment risk requires safeguards across all AI systems reaching critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: It is important that the industry adopts strategies for addressing this risk: what is detailed in this section represents one possible approach for doing so.
units.paraphrase: Industry-wide adoption of strategies is important; this section presents one possible approach.

units.section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
units.excerpt: An initial mitigation approach focuses on detecting when models might develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which they have the potential to undermine human control, assuming no additional mitigations were applied.
units.paraphrase: The initial approach focuses on detecting a baseline instrumental reasoning ability that could enable undermining human control absent mitigations.

units.section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
units.excerpt: When models reach this capability level, we believe applying an automated monitor to the model’s explicit reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought output) is an effective mitigation.
units.paraphrase: At this capability level, automated monitoring of explicit reasoning output is believed to be an effective mitigation.

units.section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
units.excerpt: Once a model is capable of effective instrumental reasoning in ways that cannot be monitored, additional mitigations may be warranted—the development of which is an area of active research.
units.paraphrase: Once instrumental reasoning becomes unmonitorable, additional mitigations, still under active research, may be needed.

units.section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
units.locator: Table 2 / Instrumental Reasoning Level 1 / Deceptive Alignment CCL
units.context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1. Column: Deceptive Alignment CCL
units.excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1: the instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness (ability to work out and use relevant details of its deployment setting) and stealth (ability to circumvent basic oversight mechanisms) such that, absent additional mitigations, we cannot rule out the model significantly undermining human control.
units.paraphrase: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1 is defined by sufficient situational awareness and stealth that, without mitigations, the model might significantly undermine human control.

units.section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
units.context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1. Column: Mitigation
units.excerpt: Automated monitoring: a monitoring system to detect illicit use of instrumental reasoning capabilities in a model’s chain-of-thought and use it in high-stakes deployments where there is significant risk of the model undermining human control.
units.paraphrase: Mitigation is automated monitoring of chain-of-thought to detect illicit instrumental reasoning use in high-stakes deployments.

units.section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
units.locator: Table 2 / Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 / Deceptive Alignment CCL
units.context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2. Column: Deceptive Alignment CCL
units.excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2: the instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness and stealth that, even when relevant model outputs (including, e.g., scratchpads) are being monitored, we cannot detect or rule out the risk of a model significantly undermining human control.
units.paraphrase: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 is defined by capability sufficient that even monitored outputs cannot detect or rule out significant undermining of human control.

units.section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
units.context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2. Column: Mitigation
units.excerpt: Future work: We are actively researching approaches to addressing models that reach this CCL.
units.paraphrase: For this CCL, mitigation approaches are still under active research.

units.excerpt: Looking forward, we expect the approach to deceptive alignment risks to take a similar form as the deployment mitigation process.
units.paraphrase: The deceptive alignment approach is expected to resemble the deployment mitigation process.

units.excerpt: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
units.paraphrase: This introduces recommended actions for AI developers for each deceptive alignment risk.

units.context_stem: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
units.excerpt: Develop a safety case based on the model’s capabilities and the mitigations applied and tested.
units.paraphrase: Developers should build a safety case based on model capabilities and tested mitigations.

units.context_stem: Develop a safety case based on the model’s capabilities and the mitigations applied and tested.
units.excerpt: Such safety cases would make the case that the likelihood of deceptive alignment risk would be low enough for safe deployment, even if the model were trying to meaningfully undermine human control.
units.paraphrase: The safety case would argue the risk of deceptive alignment is low enough for safe deployment even under adversarial assumptions.

units.context_stem: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
units.excerpt: Test the mitigations applied to models via red-teaming protocols called “control evaluations,” to determine whether they meet the requirements of the safety case.
units.paraphrase: Developers should test mitigations via control evaluations to see if they meet the safety case's requirements.

units.excerpt: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
units.paraphrase: The approach depends on two distinct safety case claims.

units.context_stem: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
units.excerpt: A model does not meet a threshold CCL and therefore would be incapable of substantially undermining human control.
units.paraphrase: Claim one: the model does not meet a threshold CCL and thus cannot substantially undermine human control.

units.context_stem: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
units.excerpt: An automated monitoring process that is validated by a control evaluation is adequate for catching the model’s malicious behavior.
units.paraphrase: Claim two: a control-evaluation-validated automated monitoring process is adequate to catch malicious behavior.

units.excerpt: Once neither of these apply, that is, once automated monitoring is no longer adequate/can no longer pass a control evaluation, a model is deemed to have reached the second CCL.
units.paraphrase: When neither safety case applies (monitoring no longer adequate or fails control evaluation), the model is deemed to have reached the second CCL.

units.excerpt: For Google models, when alert thresholds are reached, the response plan will be reviewed and approved by appropriate corporate governance bodies such as the Google DeepMind AGI Safety Council, Google DeepMind Responsibility and Safety Council, and/or Google Trust & Compliance Council.
units.paraphrase: Upon alert threshold triggers, the response plan is reviewed and approved by named corporate governance bodies.

units.excerpt: The Google DeepMind AGI Safety Council will periodically review the implementation of the Framework.
units.paraphrase: The AGI Safety Council will periodically review Framework implementation.

units.excerpt: If we assess that a model has reached a CCL that poses an unmitigated and material risk to overall public safety, we aim to share information with appropriate government authorities where it will facilitate the development of safe AI.
units.paraphrase: If a CCL poses unmitigated material risk to public safety, Google aims to share information with relevant government authorities.

units.excerpt: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
units.paraphrase: This introduces categories of information that may be disclosed, subject to confidentiality safeguards.

units.excerpt: Model information: characteristics of the AI model relevant to the risk it may pose with its critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: One disclosable category is model information relevant to the risk posed by its critical capabilities.

units.context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
units.excerpt: Evaluation results: such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests.
units.paraphrase: Another disclosable category is evaluation results, including design, results, and robustness tests.

units.context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
units.excerpt: Mitigation plans: descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk.
units.paraphrase: Another disclosable category is mitigation plans and their expected risk reduction.

units.excerpt: We may also consider disclosing information to other external organizations to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.
units.paraphrase: Disclosure to other external organizations may also be considered to promote shared learning and coordinated mitigation.

units.excerpt: We will continue to review and evolve our disclosure process over time.
units.paraphrase: The disclosure process will continue to be reviewed and evolved.

units.excerpt: We expect the Framework to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves, and we will publish substantive revisions as appropriate.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is expected to evolve substantially, with substantive revisions published as appropriate.

units.paraphrase: This introduces a list of issues planned for future Framework versions.

units.excerpt: Greater precision in risk modeling: While we have updated our CCLs and underlying threat models from version 1.0, there remains significant room for improvement in understanding the risks posed by models in different domains, and refining our set of CCLs.
units.paraphrase: Future work includes greater precision in risk modeling, despite updates since version 1.0, as room remains for improved understanding and CCL refinement.

units.context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
units.excerpt: Capability elicitation: Our evaluators continue to improve their ability to estimate what capabilities may be attainable by different threat actors with access to our models, taking into account a growing number of possible post-training enhancements.
units.paraphrase: Future work includes improving estimation of attainable capabilities by threat actors, accounting for post-training enhancements.

units.context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:

units.paraphrase: Future work may address additional risk domains and critical capabilities as AI capabilities and the external environment evolve.

units.context_stem: Updated set of risks and mitigations: There may be additional risk domains and critical capabilities that fall into scope as AI capabilities improve and the external environment changes.
units.excerpt: Future work will aim to include additional pressing risks, which may include additional risk domains or higher CCLs within existing domains.
units.paraphrase: Future work aims to add pressing risks, possibly new domains or higher CCLs within existing domains.

units.paraphrase: Future work includes deceptive alignment approaches beyond automated monitoring, actively researched for the Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 CCL.

units.context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
units.excerpt: Broader approach to ML R&D risks: The risks posed by models reaching our ML R&D CCLs may require measures beyond security and deployment mitigations, to ensure that safety measures and social institutions continue to be able to adapt to new AI capabilities amidst possible acceleration in AI development.
units.paraphrase: ML R&D CCL risks may require measures beyond security and deployment mitigations to keep safety measures and institutions adaptive amid accelerating AI development.

units.paraphrase: Appropriate responses to these ML R&D risk scenarios are being actively researched.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from the high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework is a set of protocols meant to address severe risks from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.

excerpt: It complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enables AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements Google's broader AI safety practices and supports innovation consistent with its AI Principles.

excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks. The core components of such Frameworks are to:
paraphrase: The Framework draws on the wider discourse about Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks, whose core components are listed below.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Identify capability levels at which frontier AI models, without additional mitigations, could pose severe risk.
paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels at which models could pose severe risk absent mitigations.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels throughout the model lifecycle.
paraphrase: Another core component is implementing protocols to detect when such capability levels are reached across the model's lifecycle.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Prepare and articulate proactive mitigation plans to ensure severe risks are adequately mitigated when such capability levels are attained.
paraphrase: Another core component is preparing proactive mitigation plans to adequately address severe risks once capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Where required or appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide the approach.
paraphrase: Another core component is involving external parties to inform and guide the approach where required or appropriate.

excerpt: In the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which frontier AI models may pose severe risks (which we call "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)"), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
paraphrase: The document specifies detection protocols for capability thresholds called CCLs and articulates mitigation approaches to address the risks they pose.

excerpt: The Framework addresses misuse risk, risks from machine learning research and development (ML R&D), and misalignment risk. For each type of risk, we define a set of CCLs and a mitigation approach for them.
paraphrase: The Framework covers misuse, ML R&D, and misalignment risks, each with its own CCLs and mitigation approach.

excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
paraphrase: Risk assessment must evaluate cross-cutting capabilities including agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

excerpt: The safety and security of frontier AI models is a global public good. The protocols here represent our current understanding and approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: Frontier AI safety and security is framed as a global public good, and the document reflects current thinking on anticipating and addressing severe risks.

excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly adopted across frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.

excerpt: These mitigations are most effective when adopted by industry as a whole: our adoption of them would result in effective risk mitigation for society only if all relevant organisations provide similar levels of protection.
paraphrase: These mitigations are most effective when adopted industry-wide, since unilateral adoption alone does not produce effective societal risk mitigation.

excerpt: The Framework is based on early and evolving research. We may change our approach over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
paraphrase: The Framework rests on early, evolving research, and the approach may change as understanding of future model capabilities improves.

excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
paraphrase: The Framework will be reviewed periodically and is expected to change substantially as understanding of risks and benefits improves.

excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/faisc, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy, https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/publications/#technical-reports.
paraphrase: Footnote lists external reference sources on frontier AI safety frameworks.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that misuse risk refers to threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.

excerpt: Misalignment can pose a number of risks. In the context of the Framework, we address specific scenarios where general-purpose AI agents are potentially misaligned and can become difficult to control, thereby posing a risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that misalignment risk in this document concerns scenarios where misaligned general-purpose AI agents become hard to control and pose severe harm.

excerpt: This section describes the central components of the Frontier Safety Framework. These protocols represent our current understanding of and approach for how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: This section introduces the central components of the Framework, reflecting current thinking on anticipating and addressing severe risks.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework targets possible severe risks arising from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.

excerpt: The Framework complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, which address other risks in addition to the severe risks in scope of the Framework in accordance with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework works alongside Google's broader AI safety practices, which address risks beyond the Framework's scope in line with AI Principles.

excerpt: The approaches and mitigations outlined in the Framework are not exclusive to models where we believe a severe risk could arise and are part of Google's comprehensive AI responsibility and safety practices.
paraphrase: Framework mitigations are not limited only to models believed to pose severe risk, and form part of Google's overall AI safety practices.

excerpt: The Framework is built around capability thresholds called "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)." These are capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models or systems may pose heightened risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: The Framework centers on CCLs, thresholds at which unmitigated models could pose heightened severe harm risk.

excerpt: CCLs are determined by identifying and analyzing the main foreseeable paths through which a model could result in severe harm: we then define the CCLs as the minimal set of capabilities a model must possess to do so.
paraphrase: CCLs are set by analyzing foreseeable severe-harm pathways and defining the minimal capabilities needed to enable them.

excerpt: We describe three sets of CCLs: misuse CCLs, machine learning R&D CCLs, and misalignment CCLs.
paraphrase: There are three CCL categories: misuse, ML R&D, and misalignment.

excerpt: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
paraphrase: Lead-in stating that misuse CCLs are defined across the following risk domains.

context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: CBRN: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear ("CBRN") threat.
paraphrase: CBRN domain covers risks of models assisting with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear threats.

context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Cyber: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a cyber attack.
paraphrase: Cyber domain covers risks of models assisting with cyber attacks.

context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Harmful Manipulation: Risks of models with high manipulative capabilities potentially being misused in ways that could reasonably result in large scale harm.
paraphrase: Harmful manipulation domain covers risks of highly manipulative models being misused to cause large scale harm.

excerpt: For machine learning R&D risk, we define CCLs that identify when ML R&D capabilities in our models may, if not properly managed, reduce society's overall ability to manage AI risks.
paraphrase: ML R&D CCLs identify when model capabilities could, if mismanaged, reduce society's ability to manage AI risks.

excerpt: Such capabilities may serve as a substantial cross-cutting risk factor for other pathways to severe harm.
paraphrase: ML R&D capabilities can act as a significant cross-cutting risk factor across other severe-harm pathways.

excerpt: For misalignment risk, we outline an exploratory approach that focuses on detecting when models might develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which they have the potential to undermine human control, assuming no additional mitigations were applied.
paraphrase: Misalignment risk is addressed via an exploratory approach focused on detecting baseline instrumental reasoning ability that could undermine human control absent mitigations.

excerpt: Most CCLs define one important component of our risk acceptance criteria. Because the CCLs for misalignment risk are exploratory and intended for illustration only, we do not associate them with explicit risk acceptance criteria.
paraphrase: Most CCLs contribute to risk acceptance criteria, but misalignment CCLs, being exploratory and illustrative, lack explicit acceptance criteria.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: For each risk domain, we conduct aspects of our risk assessment at various moments throughout the model development process, both before and after deployment.
paraphrase: Risk assessment occurs at multiple points throughout model development, both pre- and post-deployment, for each risk domain.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: We conduct a risk assessment for the first external deployment of a new frontier AI model.
paraphrase: A risk assessment is conducted for a new frontier model's first external deployment.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: For subsequent versions of the model, we conduct a further risk assessment if the model has meaningful new capabilities or a material increase in performance, until the model is retired or we deploy a more capable model.
paraphrase: For later model versions, another risk assessment is triggered by meaningful new capabilities or material performance increases, continuing until retirement or replacement by a more capable model.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: The reason for this is because a material change in the model's capabilities may mean that the risk profile of the model has changed or the justification for why the risks stemming from the model are acceptable has been materially undermined.
paraphrase: This is because capability changes may alter the model's risk profile or undermine the justification for accepting its risks.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: To identify meaningful new capabilities or material increases in performance, we conduct model capability evaluations, including our automated benchmarks.
paraphrase: Model capability evaluations, including automated benchmarks, are used to identify meaningful new capabilities or performance increases.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: These evaluations are primarily aimed at understanding the capabilities of the model and may be triggered, for example, upon the completion of a pre-training or post-training run, on various candidates of a model version.
paraphrase: Evaluations primarily aim to understand model capabilities and may be triggered by events like completion of pre-training or post-training runs on model candidates.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: These evaluations include a broad range of areas, including general capability evaluations, model behavior, efficiency, coding capabilities, multilinguality, or reasoning.
paraphrase: The evaluations cover a wide range of areas such as general capability, behavior, efficiency, coding, multilinguality and reasoning.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: Data from these evaluations are collected and analyzed to give us an indication as to how the model is performing and whether a risk assessment is necessary.
paraphrase: Evaluation data is collected and analyzed to indicate model performance and whether a risk assessment is needed.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps (which do not need to be repeated where a previous risk assessment is still appropriate):
paraphrase: Lead-in introducing the high-level steps of the risk assessment process.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
excerpt: Identification: As explained above, we have identified risk domains where, based on early research, we have determined severe risks may be most likely to arise from future models: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and machine learning R&D.
paraphrase: The Identification step names the domains where severe risks are most likely: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and ML R&D.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
excerpt: As part of our broader research into frontier AI models, we continue to assess whether there are other risk domains where severe risks may arise and will update our approach as appropriate. For each of the four identified domains, we have developed specific scenarios in which these risks could materialize.
paraphrase: Ongoing research continues to assess whether additional risk domains exist, with the approach updated accordingly, and specific scenarios have been developed for each of the four identified domains.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
excerpt: Analysis: Central to our model evaluations are "early warning evaluations," to assess the proximity of the model to a CCL. We define "alert thresholds" for these evaluations that are designed to flag when a CCL may be reached before a risk assessment is conducted again.
paraphrase: The Analysis step centers on early warning evaluations with alert thresholds designed to flag approaching CCLs between risk assessments.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to equip the model with appropriate scaffolding and other augmentations to make it more likely that we are also assessing the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model.
paraphrase: Evaluations aim to include appropriate scaffolding and augmentations so that assessments capture likely downstream system capabilities too.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust the alert threshold of our evaluations if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: Evaluation frequency or alert thresholds may be adjusted if progress suggests the safety buffer is inadequate.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
excerpt: We conduct further analysis, including reviewing model independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.
paraphrase: Further analysis includes reviewing independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
excerpt: Acceptance determination and mitigations: We then determine whether the model has met or will meet a CCL and, if so, whether we need to implement any further mitigations to reduce the risk to an acceptable level (see below).
paraphrase: This step determines whether the model has met or will meet a CCL and whether further mitigations are needed to reach an acceptable risk level.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: Our approach to model evaluations and risk assessments described above means we can proactively monitor a model's capabilities throughout the entire lifecycle of the model and ensure that any severe risk is properly identified and mitigated.
paraphrase: This approach enables proactive monitoring of model capabilities throughout its lifecycle to ensure severe risks are identified and mitigated.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: Where appropriate, we may engage relevant and appropriate external actors, including governments, to inform our responsible development and deployment practices.
paraphrase: External actors, including governments, may be engaged where appropriate to inform responsible development and deployment.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / fn4
excerpt: We exclude misalignment risk from this list of domains because of its exploratory nature.
paraphrase: Misalignment risk is excluded from the listed risk domains due to its exploratory status.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
excerpt: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs: Risk assessment must take into account the fact that other actors may put significantly more effort into eliciting capabilities than we put into assessing risk, thus requiring conservatism in the form of evaluations.
paraphrase: Risk assessment for ML R&D CCLs must factor in that other actors may elicit capabilities harder than internal risk assessment efforts, requiring conservative evaluation.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
excerpt: However, as a frontier AI company, we do not expect other groups to put significantly more effort into ML R&D than we do ourselves.
paraphrase: As a frontier AI company, GDM does not expect others to invest significantly more effort in ML R&D than it does.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
excerpt: As a result, to assess the ML R&D CCLs, we may use sources of information about our own progress at accelerating ML R&D to assess whether we are near or at the CCLs, in addition to evaluations of ML R&D capabilities.
paraphrase: Assessment of ML R&D CCLs may draw on internal progress data on accelerating ML R&D, alongside capability evaluations.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
excerpt: Similarly, our alert threshold may be defined based on these sources of information, rather than on evaluation scores.
paraphrase: Alert thresholds for ML R&D may similarly be defined using such internal progress information rather than evaluation scores.

excerpt: We apply safety and security mitigations throughout the lifecycle of our models, including as part of our training and model development phase and, where appropriate, before CCLs are reached as described in the process below.
paraphrase: Safety and security mitigations are applied throughout the model lifecycle, including during training and development, and before CCLs are reached where appropriate.

excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: Reaching an alert threshold triggers assessment of proximity to the CCL and risk analysis, involving internal and external experts as needed.

excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.

excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse CCLs (CBRN, cyber and harmful manipulation), as well as the mitigation approach that we assess as appropriate for them.

paraphrase: Two mitigation categories address misuse-critical models: security mitigations against weight exfiltration, and deployment mitigations against misuse in external deployments.

excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the appropriateness and robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
paraphrase: Multiple security mitigation levels allow calibration of measures' appropriateness and robustness to the risks posed.

excerpt: For deployment mitigations, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: A standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing deployment mitigations aims to calibrate them to CCLs, reflecting their iterative, CCL-dependent nature.

excerpt: This structured process for deployment mitigations is centered on assessing and reviewing that the risk of severe harm has been brought to an appropriate level proportionate to the risk.
paraphrase: The deployment mitigations process centers on assessing and reviewing that severe harm risk has been reduced proportionately.

excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration risk, such as identity and access management practices and hardening interface-access to unreleased model parameters, are important for models reaching CCLs.
paraphrase: Security mitigations against exfiltration, such as access management and hardening interfaces to unreleased parameters, are important for CCL-reaching models.

excerpt: This is because the release of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Releasing model weights could allow removal of trained-in or deployed safeguards, giving threat actors access to critical capabilities.

excerpt: Here, we use security levels that indicate goals/principles in line with the corresponding level in the RAND framework.
paraphrase: Security levels here align with goals and principles at the corresponding level in the RAND framework.

excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
paraphrase: As AI security is actively researched, concrete measures for reaching each security level are expected to evolve substantially.

excerpt: In other words, "security level N" indicates security controls and detections at a level generally aligned with RAND SL N. See https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html, pp 21-22.
paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that 'security level N' aligns generally with RAND SL N and cites the source pages.

paraphrase: Alignment with RAND refers to goals and principles, not the concrete benchmark measures described in the RAND report.

excerpt: As the authors point out, the "security level benchmarks represent neither a complete standard nor a compliance regime—they are provided for informational purposes only and should inform security teams' decisions rather than supersede them."
paraphrase: Footnote quotes RAND authors stating the security level benchmarks are informational only, not a complete standard or compliance regime.

paraphrase: Mitigations are considered adequate when evidence shows the increased likelihood of severe harm has been reduced to an acceptable level.

excerpt: Post-deployment processes: our safety cases and mitigations may be updated if deemed necessary by post-market monitoring. Material updates to a safety case will be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review.
paraphrase: Post-deployment, safety cases and mitigations may be updated based on monitoring, and material updates require governance review.

excerpt: This process is designed to ensure that residual risk remains at acceptable levels: evidence of efficacy collected during development and testing, as well as expert-driven estimates of other parameters, will enable us to assess residual risk and to detect substantial changes that invalidate our risk assessment.
paraphrase: The process aims to keep residual risk acceptable by using efficacy evidence and expert estimates to assess risk and detect invalidating changes.

excerpt: With iteration on safeguards and safety cases, we believe that we are able to make informed decisions about the level of risk via a CCL before a model is released or deployed internally at scale, and reliably prevent models posing unacceptable levels of risk from being deployed.
paraphrase: Iterating on safeguards and safety cases is believed to enable informed risk decisions before release and reliably block unacceptably risky models from deployment.

excerpt: The table below details a set of ML R&D CCLs we have identified that may lead to heightened severe risk through ML R&D. We expect these to evolve over time.
paraphrase: The table lists identified ML R&D CCLs that could lead to heightened severe risk, expected to evolve over time.

excerpt: We recommend a security level for each of these CCLs, which reflect our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.
paraphrase: A security level is recommended for each CCL, reflecting the assessed minimum appropriate security the frontier AI field should apply.

excerpt: These CCLs focus on risks posed by models capable of accelerating the rate of AI progress.
paraphrase: This subsection's CCLs address risks from models that can accelerate AI progress.

excerpt: These capabilities may indicate a heightened ability to undermine human control of models, may incentivize greater (and therefore higher risk) deployment of models, and could also result in the unsafe attainment or proliferation of other powerful AI models if misused by external threat actors.
paraphrase: Such capabilities may signal increased ability to undermine human control, incentivize riskier deployment, and enable unsafe proliferation of powerful models if misused.

excerpt: Therefore, we recommend models at this level of capability have exceptional security even though they may have substantial innovation costs.
paraphrase: Exceptional security is recommended for this capability level despite potentially substantial innovation costs.

paraphrase: Footnote 16 explains this level may include SL 2 and 3 mitigations plus measures to isolate model weights, enhance data center security, harden infrastructure, and minimize attack surface.

excerpt: Misalignment can pose a number of risks. In the context of the Framework, we address specific scenarios where general-purpose AI agents are potentially misaligned and can become difficult to control, thereby posing a risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: Misalignment poses several risks; the Framework addresses scenarios where misaligned general-purpose AI agents become difficult to control, risking severe harm.

excerpt: Here we describe an approach for addressing misalignment risk that focuses specifically on when models may develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which, without additional mitigations, they may have the potential to undermine human control.
paraphrase: The approach focuses on the point at which models develop baseline instrumental reasoning ability that could, absent mitigations, undermine human control.

excerpt: When models reach this capability level, one possible mitigation is to apply an automated monitor to the model's explicit reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought output).
paraphrase: One possible mitigation upon reaching this capability level is applying an automated monitor to the model's explicit reasoning output.

excerpt: Once a model is capable of effective instrumental reasoning in ways that cannot be monitored, additional mitigations may be warranted—the development of which is an area of active research.
paraphrase: Once instrumental reasoning becomes unmonitorable, further mitigations may be needed, and developing them is an active research area.

excerpt: Given its nascency, we expect our approach to misalignment risk to evolve substantially. This section is therefore illustrative only.
paraphrase: Because the approach is nascent, it is expected to evolve substantially, and this section is illustrative only.

excerpt: Accordingly, we do not indicate security mitigations for models at these CCLs. The table below summarizes the initial approach:
paraphrase: No security mitigations are indicated for models at these CCLs, and the table summarizes the initial approach.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework will be updated at least once a year—more frequently if we have reasonable grounds to believe the adequacy of the Framework or our adherence to it has been materially undermined.
paraphrase: The Framework will be updated at least annually, or more often if there is reason to believe its adequacy or adherence has been materially undermined.

excerpt: The process will involve (i) an assessment of the Framework's appropriateness for the management of systemic risk, drawing on information sources such as record of adherence to the framework, relevant high-quality research, information shared through industry forums, and evaluation results, as necessary, and (ii) an assessment of our adherence to the Framework.
paraphrase: The update process includes assessing the Framework's appropriateness using various information sources, and assessing GDM's own adherence to it.

excerpt: Following this assessment, we may:
paraphrase: The following list describes possible actions following the assessment.

excerpt: Update our risk domains and CCLs, where necessary.
paraphrase: Risk domains and CCLs may be updated as necessary.

excerpt: Update our testing and mitigation approaches, where needed to ensure risk remains adequately assessed and addressed according to our current understanding.
paraphrase: Testing and mitigation approaches may be updated as needed to ensure risk continues to be adequately assessed and addressed.

excerpt: The updated version and framework assessment will be reviewed by the appropriate corporate governance bodies.
paraphrase: Corporate governance bodies will review the updated version and framework assessment.

excerpt: If we assess that a model has reached a CCL that poses an unmitigated and material risk to overall public safety, we aim to share relevant information with appropriate government authorities where it will facilitate safety of frontier AI.
paraphrase: If a model reaches a CCL posing unmitigated material risk to public safety, GDM aims to share relevant information with government authorities where it aids frontier AI safety.

excerpt: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:

paraphrase: One category of shareable information is model characteristics relevant to its critical-capability risk.

excerpt: Evaluation results: such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests.
paraphrase: Another category is evaluation results, including design details, results, and robustness tests.

excerpt: Mitigation plans: descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk.
paraphrase: The third category is mitigation plan descriptions and their expected risk-reduction effects.

excerpt: We may also consider disclosing information to other external organisations to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.
paraphrase: GDM may also consider disclosing information to other external organisations to support shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.

excerpt: We will continue to review and evolve our disclosure process over time.
paraphrase: The disclosure process will continue to be reviewed and evolved over time.
